title: The Effects of Outdoor Air Supply Rate in an Office on Perceived Air Quality, Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) Symptoms and Productivity
authors: Pawel Wargocki, David P. Wyon, Jan Sundell, Geo Clausen and P. Ole Fanger

participants.demographics: female students, 18-33 years old (mean 23.5±3.4 years), 168±6 cm, 63±9.5 kg. 5 smokers (<6 cig./day), 7 subjects sensitive to poor air quality, 23 with SBS history.
participants.sampling_strategy: recruited to participate, familiar with PC, no chronic diseases

independent_variables.name: Outdoor air supply rate
independent_variables.description: Corresponding to air change rates of 0.6, 2, or 6 h⁻¹.

dependent_variables: Perceived air quality (acceptability, freshness, odour intensity, nose irritation)
SBS symptoms (dryness of mouth and throat, difficulty in thinking clearly, general feeling of wellbeing, fatigue, depression, throat irritation)
Productivity (text typing, addition, proof-reading, creative thinking)
controlled_variables: Extra pollution source (carpet strips, 36 m² surface area)
data_collection_methods: Questionnaires (perceived air quality, general perceptions of indoor climate, SBS symptoms, effort, thermal comfort, noise acceptability, thermal environment acceptability)
Simulated office work tasks (text typing, addition, proof-reading, creative thinking)
Physical/chemical measurements (airflow, ventilation effectiveness, SF6, CO2, TVOC, O3, formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, C5-C10 aldehydes, temperature, RH, noise level)
study_design.statistical_analysis: Shapiro-Wilk test for normality, non-parametric 1-tailed Page test for ordered alternatives, linear regression (log-transformed ventilation rate for performance)

practical_implications: Good indoor air quality is beneficial for health, comfort and productivity.
Ventilate indoor environments at rates above minimum levels prescribed in present standards and guidelines.
Reducing costs and conserving energy by maintaining modest levels of ventilation can easily result in a net loss if productivity is decreased.
Increasing ventilation rates above minimum levels can raise productivity and will, in many cases, pay for itself while decreasing the intensity of SBS symptoms and improving perceived air quality.
Intelligent use of energy recovery can often minimize energy consumption caused by increased ventilation.

As an alternative or supplement to increased ventilation, it will often be beneficial for indoor air quality to eliminate or reduce sources of indoor air pollution or to supply ventilation air close to the breathing zone of the occupants.
limitations: Study used young female students, who consistently report more SBS symptoms than males.
Subjects were exposed only once to each condition for ca. 4.6 h, unlike repeated exposures for 8 h per day and 5 days per week in real workplaces.
The office environment, though natural, may have been perceived as different from a normal workplace.
The 'necessary effort' scale was difficult for subjects to use and its interpretation ambiguous, suggesting it should not be used in its present form.

paper_metadata.title: The effects of outdoor air supply rate in an office on perceived air quality, sick building syndrome (SBS) symptoms and productivity.
paper_metadata.journal: Indoor Air: International Journal of Indoor Environment and Health

environmental_features: outdoor air supply rate (e.g., 3 L/s per person, 10 L/s per person, 30 L/s per person)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: continuous 8-hour workday, with subjects exposed to each condition for multiple days (e.g., 5 days per condition)
control_conditions: different outdoor air supply rates served as comparison conditions against each other

mechanism_chain.description: Increased outdoor air supply dilutes indoor pollutants, leading to improved perceived air quality, reduced SBS symptoms, and consequently enhanced productivity.

steps.to_construct: concentration of indoor pollutants (e.g., bioeffluents, VOCs, CO2)
sick building syndrome (SBS) symptoms (e.g., headache, eye irritation, fatigue)

instruments_used.name: Perceived Air Quality Questionnaire
instruments_used.description: Self-report scales for air acceptability, freshness, and intensity of odor (e.g., using visual analog scales)

instruments_used.name: SBS Symptom Checklist
instruments_used.description: Self-report questionnaire assessing the prevalence and intensity of various SBS symptoms (e.g., headache, dry eyes, stuffy nose, fatigue)

instruments_used.name: Standardized Office Performance Tests
instruments_used.description: Objective measures of performance on typical office tasks, such as proofreading, text typing, and addition tasks

instruments_used.name: Self-reported Productivity Scale
instruments_used.description: Self-report scale assessing perceived productivity or work performance

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Indoor environmental factors, such as air quality, can cause a range of non-specific symptoms in building occupants.
There is a quantifiable relationship between the level of an environmental stimulus (e.g., ventilation rate) and the magnitude of human response (e.g., perceived air quality, symptoms, performance).
